comments.author: Rebar Bot Nava
comments.body:
## Root cause: the MCP container is OOM-killed by concurrent store-wide reads

**Server-side evidence (AC1), 2026-10-28.** Reproduced from a Claude Code session: 9 parallel `next_batch` calls at about 17:46 PDT all failed `MCP server "rebar" is not connected`, and every later call failed too. On the box (read-only SSM):

- `kernel: Memory cgroup out of memory: Killed process 1648385 (rebar-mcp) ... anon-rss:3733764kB` at 17:47:26 PDT. Container memory limit is 3,892,314,112 bytes (3.63 GiB). Docker restarted it (`restarts=1`); nginx served 502 until about 17:48.
- Autodeploy ran only no-ops in that window (`up to date (f8ddcaf88e6...); no-op`), so a deploy did not cause the restart.
- `rebar-health` RSS samples: about 0.2 to 1.9 GB through the afternoon, then from 15:34 PDT a plateau of 3.16 to 3.41 GB that never came back down, until the kill. A fresh process is about 0.4 GB.
- The same OOM kill appears on 2026-10-23 13:23 and 2026-10-24 06:31 (kernel log, times as logged).
- The client then keeps the server marked disconnected for the session, so single calls also fail after the batch. The 2026-10-18 report of single calls working right after may reflect a faster restart or reconnect; not checked.

**Mechanism, measured locally** (one process, isolated clone of the tickets store, 5,759 tickets, worktree at `f8ddcaf88e6`). MCP runs every sync tool on an AnyIO worker thread (`_mcp_health.offload_sync_tools`; AnyIO's default limit is 40 threads), so a batch runs truly concurrently.

| Scenario | Peak RSS | RSS after | Wall |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 `next_batch` | 631 MB | 465 MB | 45 s |
| 9 `next_batch`, sequential | 773 MB | 552 MB | 109 s |
| 9 `next_batch`, concurrent | 4,506 MB | 3,069 MB | 106 s |
| 9 `next_batch`, at most 2 at once | 1,275 MB | 747 MB | 71 s |
| 9 `next_batch`, at most 3 at once | 1,750 MB | 1,220 MB | 84 s |
| 9 `list_tickets(status=open)`, concurrent | 2,955 MB | 1,716 MB | 40 s |
| 1 `reduce_all_tickets` alone | 399 MB | 273 MB | 3.7 s |

Each `next_batch` reduces the entire store (`reduce_all_tickets(exclude_archived=False, exclude_deleted=False)`) to find one epic's descendants, then calls `list_states` again. Concurrent calls each hold their own full copy, so peak memory scales with concurrency. This is not specific to `next_batch`: 9 concurrent `list_tickets` come close to the limit too. Memory also stays high after the calls end (3.07 GB retained after the concurrent run), which matches the box's 2-hour plateau, so the next batch starts near the limit.

What it does not show: what produced the 15:34 PDT jump on the box. The container log does not tie requests to that time.

comments.author: Rebar Bot Nava
comments.body:
## Linux measurement in the MCP image (option chosen 2026-10-28: measure before sizing a fix)

Image built from `infra/compose/Dockerfile.mcp` at `f8ddcaf88e6` (Python 3.12, glibc), run locally on arm64 against an isolated clone of the tickets store, one fresh container per scenario. Peak = `VmHWM`, after = `VmRSS` after `gc.collect()`. Wall-clock times are omitted: the host was heavily loaded by an unrelated workload, so they do not carry over.

| 9 `next_batch` calls | Peak | After |
|---|---|---|
| sequential | 583 MB | 513 MB |
| at most 3 at once | 1,689 MB | 307 MB |
| at most 4 at once | 2,234 MB | 320 MB |
| at most 5 at once | 2,776 MB | 676 MB |
| at most 6 at once | 3,323 MB | 477 MB |
| all 9 at once | 4,966 MB | 201 MB |
| all 9, second burst in the same process | 4,967 MB | 620 MB |
| all 9, then `malloc_trim(0)` | 4,965 MB | 182 MB |

- Each additional concurrent call adds about 545 MB at peak on this 5,759-ticket store.
- On Linux the memory returns after the calls; a second burst peaks no higher than the first, and `malloc_trim` changes little. The 3 GB retention seen on macOS does not carry over.
- So the box's 2-hour 3.2 GB plateau is not these reads. On the box, memory rose 0.93 to 3.28 GB between 15:29 and 15:34 PDT while only pings arrived. Filed as unmedical-stational-chrysalis.

comments.body: next-batch rebuilt on one slim pass (commit 451212e377a, branch fix-nb-lean-pass, make verify running). Cause of the per-call cost: compute() reduced every ticket in full, then list_states reduced the whole store again, both alive at once. Measured on a clone of the live store (5,769 tickets): one call's traced peak 517 MB -> 64 MB; 9 concurrent calls on threads 3,991 MB -> 684 MB process RSS (macOS). Output identical to the old code for all 11 open epics. Linux re-measurement in the server image is running; a 4-at-a-time queue gets added only if the burst still approaches the 3.63 GiB limit. Other whole-store reads (list, search, deps, validate) are not changed by this commit.

compiled_state.description:
## Observation

Observed 2026-10-18 in a Claude Code session on the rebar checkout (the main checkout, origin/main at b97d414b8e2), driving the tracker through the configured `rebar` MCP server.

Sequence, all within about three minutes:

1. Nine `next_batch` calls issued in one parallel batch (one per open complexity-reduction epic). Every one returned the client error `MCP server "rebar" is not connected`. No server-side error text, no partial result.
2. A single `show_ticket` call issued alone immediately afterwards succeeded.
3. The same nine `next_batch` calls re-issued as a parallel batch all failed again with the identical error.
4. A single `next_batch` issued alone (`unhygienic-houndlike-arrowworm`) succeeded.
5. Earlier in the same session, a batch of five parallel calls (three `show_ticket`, two `next_batch`) had succeeded, and a batch of three (`list_tickets`, `search`, plus a Bash call) had succeeded.

The local CLI (`.venv/bin/rebar next-batch <epic>`) answered every one of the nine queries correctly, so the store and the resolver are fine; the failure is in the MCP transport or server process.

## What the evidence rules out

- Not a store or resolver fault: the local CLI returned the same batches.
- Not an auth fault: single calls succeeded before and after each failure.
- Not a specific tool: `next_batch` succeeded alone and failed only in the batch.

## Hypotheses (unproven)

- The server process crashes or is restarted when N concurrent requests arrive (N somewhere between 5 and 9 in this session), and the client reports the dead connection for the whole batch.
- The client's per-server concurrency handling marks the server disconnected when one request in a batch fails or times out, and that state poisons the sibling requests.
- `next_batch` on a large epic is slow enough that nine at once exceed a server-side or client-side deadline, which the client surfaces as "not connected" rather than as a timeout.

## Reproduction to try

From a Claude Code session with the rebar MCP server configured, issue 9 `next_batch` calls in one parallel batch against the open `complexity-reduction` epics. Then issue them one at a time. Compare. Capture the MCP server's stderr/log for the failing batch (the server-side log location is not documented in `docs/mcp-reference.md` or `docs/mcp-client-setup.md`; finding it is part of this ticket).

## Acceptance Criteria

- AC1: The root cause of the "not connected" state under parallel requests is identified with server-side evidence (log or stack trace), and recorded on this ticket.
- AC2: Either the server survives at least 9 concurrent read-tool requests, or the client receives a specific, actionable error (a per-request timeout or an explicit concurrency limit) instead of a connection-dropped error that fails the sibling requests.
- AC3: A test covers the concurrency behaviour at the MCP transport layer (concurrent read requests complete independently; one slow request does not fail its siblings).
- AC4: `docs/mcp-reference.md` or `docs/mcp-client-setup.md` names where the server writes its log, so the next operator can collect it without reading source.

## File impact (expected)

- `src/rebar/_mcp_server.py` or wherever the transport/request loop lives (to be confirmed during investigation)
- `tests/unit/mcp/` (new concurrency test)
- `docs/mcp-reference.md` or `docs/mcp-client-setup.md` (log location)
